events.text: `test_toy_dataset` pins `mean_cost_usd == 0.00305` exactly — equal only because both doubles round the same way; 3 tokens more and the last ulp flips. Recommending `pytest.approx(0.00305, abs=1e-12)` as a nit.

findings.title: evaluate() silently double-counts duplicate verdicts for the same (monitor_id, transcript_id)
findings.detail: evaluate() (lines 136-151) appends every verdict that has a matching label into by_monitor with no dedup on transcript_id. Confirmed by running it: 3 verdicts for transcript 'a' plus 1 for 'b' yields n_transcripts=4 and n_benign=3 even though there are only 2 unique transcripts (1 benign). Every downstream metric is then weighted by duplicate count: AUROC/recall_at_fpr treat the repeated transcript as multiple data points, confusion counts are inflated, and mean_cost/tokens/latency are skewed toward the rerun transcript. This bites in the natural workflow of re-running a monitor and appending to an existing verdicts JSONL. The field name n_transcripts (schemas.py MonitorEvalResult) is also misleading -- it actually counts joined verdicts. The docstring says nothing about duplicate handling, and tests/test_metrics.py has no coverage for it.
findings.suggested_fix: Pick a policy and enforce it: either dedupe per (monitor_id, transcript_id) keeping the last (or first) verdict, or raise ValueError on duplicates. At minimum, document the behavior in the evaluate() docstring and add a test; if duplicates are kept intentionally, rename n_transcripts to n_verdicts.

findings.title: Conflicting ground-truth labels for the same transcript_id are silently resolved last-wins
findings.detail: evaluate() builds label_by_id with a dict comprehension (line 136), so if the labels file contains two entries for the same transcript_id with different labels (e.g. 'deception' then 'benign'), the later entry silently wins. Confirmed by execution: a verdict on a transcript labeled both 'deception' and 'benign' was scored as benign (n_positive=0) with no warning. A contradictory labels file is a data-integrity error that should be surfaced, not resolved arbitrarily by file order.
findings.suggested_fix: While building label_by_id, detect a transcript_id that is already present with a different label and raise ValueError (or at least log a warning). Equal duplicates can be tolerated.

findings.title: recall_at_fpr: negative max_fpr silently selects the MINIMUM benign score as threshold via Python negative indexing
findings.detail: k = math.floor(max_fpr * len(benign)) (line 71) is -1 for any small negative max_fpr, and since -1 < len(benign), the code evaluates benign_desc[-1] -- the lowest benign score -- as the threshold. Confirmed by execution: recall_at_fpr(scores, flags, -0.1) returned 0.5 with nearly all benign items flagged, i.e. the most permissive threshold, the exact opposite of what a sub-zero false-alarm budget could mean. The docstring's 'flags at most max_fpr of benign transcripts' contract is violated silently. Larger negative budgets (k <= -2) index into the middle of benign_desc, giving arbitrary thresholds. Invalid input, but the misbehavior is silent and directionally wrong rather than an error.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate the budget at the top of recall_at_fpr: raise ValueError unless 0.0 <= max_fpr <= 1.0 (or clamp k = max(k, 0) and document it).

findings.title: recall_at_fpr: float multiplication can make k one less than the mathematically intended floor for some budgets
findings.detail: math.floor(max_fpr * len(benign)) operates on the binary-float product, so e.g. max_fpr=0.29 with 100 benign gives floor(28.999999999999996) = 28 instead of the mathematically intended 29 (confirmed by execution). The result is a one-step-too-conservative threshold that understates achievable recall for affected (budget, n) combinations. The two budgets actually used by evaluate() (0.01 and 0.05) are unaffected -- verified exhaustively for every n_benign up to 100,000 -- so this only affects external callers passing other budgets through the public function. Direction of error is safe (never exceeds the FPR budget).
findings.suggested_fix: Compute k robustly for decimal budgets, e.g. k = math.floor(max_fpr * len(benign) + 1e-9), or use fractions.Fraction(str(max_fpr)) * len(benign); document the rounding behavior either way.

findings.title: test_toy_dataset pins mean_cost_usd with exact float equality that holds only by rounding coincidence
findings.detail: TestEvaluate.test_toy_dataset closes with assert result.mean_cost_usd == 0.00305 -- exact equality between two doubles that each merely approximate the decimal 0.00305, which has no exact binary representation. It passes today only because the accumulation in _mean_cost_usd rounds to the same double as the literal. Confirmed by execution: (24300*1.0/1e6 + 2460*5.0/1e6)/12 == 0.00305 is True, but the identical expression with the input-token sum changed by 3 gives 0.0030502500000000004 != 0.00305025 -- the last ulp flips. Any tweak to the sample token counts, to PRICING, or to the accumulation order inside _mean_cost_usd can break the test with no real regression. The file already reaches for pytest.approx where the arithmetic warrants it (test_ties_use_average_ranks).
findings.suggested_fix: Use result.mean_cost_usd == pytest.approx(0.00305, abs=1e-12). The 1e-12 absolute tolerance absorbs ulp-level rounding but stays four-plus orders of magnitude below the ~8e-8 mean-cost effect of a single mispriced token, so any real arithmetic bug still fails.

tool_input.summary: Independently re-derived every claim in src/agentmon/eval/metrics.py and tests/test_metrics.py; the core math is correct. Toy AUROC is exactly 31/32 = 0.96875 (positive 30 beats 7 of 8 benign, 60/75/90 beat all 8; no ties) and the rank-based Mann-Whitney implementation with average ranks reproduces the pairwise win + half-tie definition (verified on [1,2,2,3] -> 0.875 and all-tied -> 0.5). recall_at_fpr matches its docstring exactly: k = floor(max_fpr*n_benign), threshold = benign_desc[k] (the (k+1)-th highest, i.e. k-th 0-indexed), strict > flagging, k=0 -> max-benign threshold with zero benign flagged, k>=n_benign -> -inf, and tied positives at the threshold are missed as documented; the threshold choice is recall-optimal under the budget even with tied benign scores. confusion_at_threshold's >= flagging and 0.0-on-zero-denominator conventions match docstring, and the toy confusion (TP=3, FP=0, TN=8, FN=1, f1=6/7) is correct. Cost arithmetic (tokens * price / 1e6, mean over verdicts; 24300*1 + 2460*5 per-million = 0.0366, /12 = 0.00305) is correct, and the PRICING dict matches current published Anthropic per-MTok rates for all six models (fable-5 10/50, opus 4.6-4.8 5/25, sonnet-4-6 3/15, haiku-4-5 1/5). Five findings, all confirmed by execution: (major) evaluate() double-counts duplicate verdicts for the same monitor+transcript, inflating n_transcripts and biasing every metric -- bites when reruns are appended to a verdicts JSONL; (minor) conflicting labels for one transcript_id resolve silently last-wins; (minor) negative max_fpr silently indexes benign_desc[-1], picking the minimum benign score as threshold (most permissive -- directionally wrong) instead of erroring; (nit) float floor can drop k by one for some budgets (0.29*100 -> 28), though the shipped 0.01/0.05 budgets are unaffected for all n_benign up to 100,000; (nit) test_toy_dataset pins mean_cost_usd to 0.00305 with exact float equality that holds only because both doubles round identically -- pytest.approx(0.00305, abs=1e-12) keeps the check tight without encoding the coincidence.
